svg.title: Reference chart of glycolysis. The ten steps drawn top to bottom in two columns, every intermediate as an open-chain Fischer projection or upright condensed structure, with what each step changed tinted. Energy investment, steps 1 to 5: 1, hexokinase (glucokinase in liver and pancreatic beta cells) phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate using ATP, irreversible; 2, phosphoglucose isomerase turns G6P into fructose-6-phosphate; 3, phosphofructokinase-1 phosphorylates F6P to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate using ATP, irreversible and rate-limiting; 4, aldolase splits F-1,6-BP into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; 5, triose phosphate isomerase interconverts DHAP and G3P. Payoff, steps 6 to 10, run twice per glucose: 6, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizes G3P with NAD+ and inorganic phosphate to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and NADH; 7, phosphoglycerate kinase moves a phosphate to ADP, making ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate (substrate-level phosphorylation); 8, phosphoglycerate mutase moves the phosphate to make 2-phosphoglycerate; 9, enolase removes water to make phosphoenolpyruvate; 10, pyruvate kinase makes ATP and pyruvate, irreversible (substrate-level phosphorylation). Reversible steps are drawn as two harpoons, irreversible ones as single red arrows. Side panels: investment and payoff per glucose (−1 ATP at step 1, −1 ATP at step 3, +2 NADH at step 6, +2 ATP at step 7, +2 ATP at step 10; net +2 ATP and +2 NADH); the three irreversible steps as the control points that gluconeogenesis must bypass; substrate-level phosphorylation needs no oxygen, which is why red blood cells live on glycolysis; branch points (G6P to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway, DHAP to glycerol 3-phosphate, 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG in red blood cells, pyruvate to lactate, acetyl-CoA, oxaloacetate or alanine). Net equation: glucose + 2 ADP + 2 Pi + 2 NAD+ gives 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 H+ + 2 H2O. What happens to pyruvate: lactate dehydrogenase reduces it to lactate with NADH, regenerating NAD+ when oxygen is short (muscle, red blood cells); with oxygen the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidizes it to acetyl-CoA, NADH and CO2 in the mitochondrial matrix, irreversibly; yeast decarboxylate it to acetaldehyde and CO2 and reduce that to ethanol with NADH (humans lack pyruvate decarboxylase).
svg.text: Glucose to two pyruvate in the cytosol of every cell, with no oxygen needed: two ATP invested, four made back, and two NADH.
